title: Patient-resolved profiling of X chromosome activity by single-cell long-read phasing
description: The X chromosome contributes disproportionally to immune function, neurodevelopment and disease susceptibility, yet its activity remains difficult to quantify at single-cell resolution. In female tissues, accurate measurements of X chromosome inactivation (XCI) requires assignment of transcripts to the active and inactive X chromosomes, but human heterozygous variants are sparse and conventional short-read single cell RNA sequencing captures only a small fraction of each transcript, limiting allele-specific analysis to a small subset of genes. Although single-cell long-read sequencing substantially increases the probability of spanning informative variants, computational approaches for chromosome-scale phasing and quantitative analysis of X chromosome activity is lacking. Here we present scDaisyChain, a graph-based framework that reconstructs chromosome-scale X haplotypes directly from single cell long-read transcriptomes and generates allele-specific maps of X chromosome activity. Benchmarking against ground-truth mouse haplotypes and long-read whole-genome sequencing demonstrates accurate phasing and robust performance under human levels of heterozygosity. By leveraging transcript-spanning reads, scDaisyChain increased the number of informative X-linked genes that could be assigned to the active or inactive X chromosome by approximately sevenfold compared with short-read-compatabile constraints, enabling comprehensive chromosome-scale XCI profiling within individual donors without requiring parental genotypes, external DNA phasing information, highly skewed XCI or cohort-level aggregation. Applying scDaisyChain to human peripheral blood immune cells revealed widespread cell-type-specific variation in XCI escape, with a major divergence between myeloid and lymphoid lineages. In rheumatoid arthritis, we identified reproducible monocyte-specific dysregulation of inactive X-expression that overlapped established inflammatory gene programmes and enabled detection of autoimmune-associated XCI abnormalities in an independent patient with Sjogren’s syndrome. Finally, we show that lineage-specific XCI skew reshapes the cellular exposure of heterozygous X-linked variants and preferentialy reduces exposure of high-priority potentially deleterious alleles. Together, these results establish scDaisyChain as a powerful approach for patient-resolved analysis of X-chromosome biology and provides a framework for investigating the constribution of X-linked dosage variation to human health and disease.
